```{r s5_precluster_pca_plot, fig.height=5.4, fig.width=9.2}
    xlab = paste0("PC1 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[1]), "%)"),
    ylab = paste0("PC2 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[2]), "%)"),
    zlab = paste0("PC3 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[3]), "%)"),
    main = "View A"
  )

  scatterplot3d::scatterplot3d(
    x = pca_df_plot_pre$PC1,
    y = pca_df_plot_pre$PC2,
    z = pca_df_plot_pre$PC3,
    color = pt_col_pre,
    pch = 16,
    cex.symbols = 0.33,
    angle = 118,
    box = FALSE,
    grid = TRUE,
    xlab = paste0("PC1 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[1]), "%)"),
    ylab = paste0("PC2 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[2]), "%)"),
    zlab = paste0("PC3 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[3]), "%)"),
    main = "View B"
  )

  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste("Cluster", cluster_levels_pre),
    col = col_map_pre[cluster_levels_pre],
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.75,
    bty = "n"
  )

  mtext(
    paste0("Pre-model clusters in PCA space (static 3D views, sampled n=", n_plot_pca_pre, ")"),
    outer = TRUE,
    line = 0.35,
    cex = 0.95,
    font = 2
  )
} else {
  ggplot(pca_df_plot_pre, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = precluster)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.22, size = 0.7) +
    stat_ellipse(level = 0.70, linewidth = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
    labs(
      title = "Pre-model clusters in PCA space (2D fallback)",
      subtitle = "Install 'scatterplot3d' for static 3D views",
      x = paste0("PC1 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[1]), "%)"),
      y = paste0("PC2 (", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pca_var_pre[2]), "%)"),
      color = "Cluster"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
}
```

**Interpretation note:** PCA is a visual diagnostic only. For PDF/LaTeX, use the static 3D twin-view figure above to check whether overlap in one projection separates under rotation; residual overlap does not invalidate clustering when stability and uncertainty diagnostics are strong.

```{r s5_precluster_outcome_boxplot, fig.height=4.6, fig.width=8.8}
ggplot(precluster_cc, aes(x = precluster, y = log_lead_time, fill = precluster)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Outcome check by pre-model cluster (diagnostic only)",
    x = "Pre-model cluster",
    y = "log1p(delivery days)",
    fill = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```


This section confirms meaningful latent structure in shipment space and supports using pre-model clusters as an engineering diagnostic before mixed-effects modelling.

From model-based criteria, BIC and ICL improve up to the maximum tested range (`K=10`), so fit criteria alone do not give a clean interior optimum. Geometry gives a different signal: silhouette is highest at `K=3` (`0.350`) and declines afterward, with `K=5` (`0.282`) still slightly better than `K=4` (`0.275`) and clearly better than `K=6` (`0.250`).

Guardrail diagnostics show the expected trade-off between parsimony and segmentation detail. `K=3` has the lowest posterior uncertainty (`0.071`) and strongest minimum cluster share (`21.0%`), while `K=5` remains acceptable on both uncertainty (`0.095`) and balance (`13.2%` smallest cluster), without creating tiny clusters (`<5%`).

Stability is the strongest argument for the final choice in this experiment. Subsample ARI is highest at `K=5` (mean `0.960`, IQR `0.954` to `0.969`), compared with `K=3` (mean `0.930`) and much weaker behaviour for `K=4` (mean `0.678`). Based on this stability-priority objective, I select `K=5` as the final pre-model segmentation.

In practical terms, this means I keep a finer but still interpretable shipment-regime partition that is highly reproducible under resampling. These clusters are used as diagnostic structure to inform model engineering (heterogeneity checks and interaction ideas), not as causal evidence by themselves; confirmatory inference remains in the mixed-effects models below.


The two displays below convert the main EDA findings into decision-ready summaries: (i) how large the same-state routing gap is in raw days, and (ii) which predictors are most strongly associated with log lead time in univariate terms.

```{r}
  dplyr::group_by(route_group) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_orders = n(),
    median_days = median(lead_time_days_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_days = mean(lead_time_days_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_days = quantile(lead_time_days_raw, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(route_group)

eda_routing_gap
```

```{r fig.height=4.8, fig.width=8}
  dplyr::mutate(
    predictor = factor(predictor, levels = rev(predictor)),
    direction = if_else(cor_with_outcome >= 0, "Positive", "Negative")
  )

ggplot(y_cor_plot, aes(x = cor_with_outcome, y = predictor, color = direction)) +
```

Taken together, the EDA supports five modelling decisions for Section 5:
(1) substantial clustering by seller and customer state, motivating crossed random intercepts;
(2) a large routing contrast (same-state vs cross-state), so `is_same_state` and `is_same_region` must remain core fixed effects;
(3) moderate but non-redundant shipment predictors, so weight/volume/value/freight/items are included jointly;
(4) pre-model unsupervised structure in shipment space, with a stable \(K=5\) segmentation (highest subsample ARI among candidate \(K \in \{3,4,5,6\}\));
(5) time and theme factors are relevant controls, but should be interpreted as adjustment terms rather than primary operational levers.

This bridge is important: the clustering result is not treated as a standalone final model, but as evidence that coefficient heterogeneity is plausible. That directly motivates the `M4_c1` and `M4_c2` extensions tested in Section 5.2.5.

# 5. Modelling
## 5.1 Robust Multivariate Diagnostics


Minimum Covariance Determinant (MCD) is a robust way to estimate the multivariate center and covariance of shipment predictors, using the most central subset of observations and downweighting extremes. Mahalanobis distance then measures how far each order is from that robust center while accounting for correlation and scale across predictors (distance is in MD\(^2\) units here).

We use MCD + robust Mahalanobis distance because shipment variables are correlated and heavy-tailed, so classical covariance and Euclidean distance can be distorted by extremes. This gives a more stable outlier flag (`ship_outlier_mcd`) for robustness checks in later models.

Interpretation of plots:
- Distance plot: each vertical line is one order's robust MD\(^2\); values above the red chi-square cutoff are flagged multivariate outliers.
- QQ plot: if points follow the 45-degree line, distances are close to a multivariate-normal reference; upward tail deviations indicate more extreme orders than normal expectation.

```{r}
# Keep only a compact numeric tail profile here; distribution and geography visuals are in Sections 3.1.2 and 4.1.
orders_mod %>%
  summarise(
    n           = n(),
    mean_days   = mean(lead_time_days_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    med_days    = median(lead_time_days_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
    p90_days    = quantile(lead_time_days_raw, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    p95_days    = quantile(lead_time_days_raw, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_days    = max(lead_time_days_raw, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```


```{r}
# robust location/scale for lead time
lead_vec <- orders_mod$lead_time_days_raw

alpha_trim <- 0.1
trim_bounds <- stats::quantile(
  lead_vec,
  probs = c(alpha_trim, 1 - alpha_trim),
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)
lead_wins <- pmax(pmin(lead_vec, trim_bounds[2]), trim_bounds[1])

lead_summary <- tibble(
  mean          = mean(lead_vec, na.rm = TRUE),
  trimmed_mean  = mean(lead_vec, trim = alpha_trim, na.rm = TRUE),
  wins_mean     = base::mean(lead_wins, na.rm = TRUE),
  median        = median(lead_vec, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd            = sd(lead_vec, na.rm = TRUE),
  MAD           = mad(lead_vec, constant = 1, na.rm = TRUE),
  IQR           = IQR(lead_vec, na.rm = TRUE)
)

lead_summary
```
Location:

Mean lead time ≈ 12.6 days

Trimmed mean (10%) ≈ 11.2 days

Winsorized mean ≈ 11.7 days

Median ≈ 10.25 days

So the classical mean is about 2.3 days higher than the median and 1.4 days higher than the 10% trimmed mean. This tells us the upper tail pulls the mean noticeably upward.


Spread:

SD ≈ 9.58 days

MAD ≈ 4.16 days

IQR ≈ 8.99 days

The robust MAD is less than half the SD, again reflecting a heavy right tail.


```{r}
# Robust multivariate outliers with rank-safe, regularized MCD

ship_cols <- c("z_log_wgt", "z_log_vol",  "z_log_freight", "z_log_items")

# Build complete-case shipment matrix
ship_df <- orders_mod[, ship_cols, drop = FALSE]
ship_keep_idx <- which(stats::complete.cases(ship_df))
X <- as.matrix(ship_df[ship_keep_idx, , drop = FALSE])
storage.mode(X) <- "double"

# Remove degenerate columns and enforce full column rank
X <- X[, apply(X, 2, stats::sd) > 1e-10, drop = FALSE]
if (ncol(X) == 0L) {
  stop("All shipment predictors were dropped as near-constant.")
}

qrX <- qr(X)
if (qrX$rank == 0L) {
  stop("Shipment predictor matrix has rank 0 after QR filtering.")
}
X <- X[, qrX$pivot[seq_len(qrX$rank)], drop = FALSE]

if (nrow(X) <= ncol(X)) {
  stop("Too few complete cases for MCD after filtering (need nrow(X) > ncol(X)).")
}

# Fit MCD and regularize covariance if needed
set.seed(42)
mcd_fit <- robustbase::covMcd(X, alpha = 0.75)

S <- mcd_fit$cov
eps <- 1e-8
iter <- 0L
while ((!is.finite(rcond(S)) || rcond(S) < 1e-10) && iter < 8L) {
  S <- S + diag(eps, ncol(S))
  eps <- eps * 10
  iter <- iter + 1L
}
if (!is.finite(rcond(S)) || rcond(S) < 1e-10) {
  stop("Regularized MCD covariance is still near-singular; check predictors.")
}

# Robust Mahalanobis distances (squared) and chi-square cutoff
md_robust <- stats::mahalanobis(X, center = mcd_fit$center, cov = S)
df_md <- ncol(X)
cut_chi <- stats::qchisq(0.975, df = df_md)

# Map outlier flags back to full modelling dataset
orders_mod$ship_outlier_mcd <- FALSE
orders_mod$ship_outlier_mcd[ship_keep_idx] <- md_robust > cut_chi

outlier_share_mcd <- mean(orders_mod$ship_outlier_mcd)  # proportion flagged
outlier_share_mcd
```

The estimated outlier share is `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * outlier_share_mcd)`%. Under a 97.5% chi-square cutoff, this is clearly above the ~2.5% expected under near-Gaussian behavior, so the shipment-feature space is materially heavy-tailed.

Intuitively, it means:

- Most orders form a “normal cloud” of shipment profiles.
- About `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * outlier_share_mcd)`% sit clearly outside that cloud when considering variables jointly (not variable-by-variable).
- So our data has a meaningful minority of unusual shipment combinations (e.g., very heavy + very high freight + multi-item), which can pull classical models.

Important nuance: these are not automatically bad records; they are just atypical patterns.
Also, with a 97.5% cutoff, a near-normal dataset would flag ~2.5%, so 9.6% suggests a heavier tail than normal.

```{r s5_mcd_outlier_scatter_matrix, fig.width=8.8, fig.height=8.8}
set.seed(2026)

spm_out_vars <- c("log_lead_time", "z_log_wgt", "z_log_vol", "z_log_freight", "z_log_items")
spm_out_df <- orders_mod %>%
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(spm_out_vars), ship_outlier_mcd) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(ship_outlier_mcd)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_all(dplyr::all_of(spm_out_vars), is.finite))

idx_non <- which(!spm_out_df$ship_outlier_mcd)
idx_out <- which(spm_out_df$ship_outlier_mcd)

n_non <- min(2600L, length(idx_non))
n_out <- min(900L, length(idx_out))

idx_keep <- c(
  if (n_non > 0L) sample(idx_non, size = n_non, replace = FALSE) else integer(0),
  if (n_out > 0L) sample(idx_out, size = n_out, replace = FALSE) else integer(0)
)

if (length(idx_keep) == 0L) {
  stop("No rows available for outlier scatterplot matrix.")
}

spm_out_sample <- spm_out_df[idx_keep, , drop = FALSE]
pt_col_out <- ifelse(
  spm_out_sample$ship_outlier_mcd,
  grDevices::adjustcolor("#b91c1c", alpha.f = 0.45),
  grDevices::adjustcolor("#64748b", alpha.f = 0.22)
)

panel_cor_out <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "r=", ...) {
  usr <- par("usr")
  on.exit(par(usr))
  par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- stats::cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs")
  txt <- paste0(prefix, formatC(r, digits = digits, format = "f"))
  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = 1.0, col = "#0f766e")
}

panel_scatter_out <- function(x, y, ...) {
  points(x, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.30, col = pt_col_out)
}

pairs(
  spm_out_sample[, spm_out_vars, drop = FALSE],
  lower.panel = panel_scatter_out,
  upper.panel = panel_cor_out,
  main = paste0("MCD outlier overlay in shipment space (sample n = ", nrow(spm_out_sample), ")")
)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Non-outlier", "MCD outlier"),
  col = c("#64748b", "#b91c1c"),
  pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.9
)
```

The outlier-overlay matrix shows that MCD outliers are concentrated in the tails of the joint shipment distribution rather than forming a completely separate cloud. This supports the robustness strategy used later (robust sensitivity checks and model variants) instead of deleting all flagged observations by default.

```{r}
# Distance diagnostics for robust MD^2
plot(
  md_robust,
  type = "h",
  main = "Robust Mahalanobis distances (MCD, regularized)",
  xlab = "Observation (complete-case shipment subset)",
  ylab = "Distance^2"
)
abline(h = cut_chi, col = "red", lty = 2)

qqplot(
  stats::qchisq(ppoints(length(md_robust)), df = df_md),
  sort(md_robust),
  main = "Robust MD^2 vs Chi-square quantiles",
  xlab = "Chi-square quantiles",
  ylab = "Robust Mahalanobis distance^2"
)
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lty = 2)


```

Interpretation of the diagnostics: the QQ plot departs upward from the 45-degree reference in the right tail, so robust MD\(^2\) values are heavier-tailed than a chi-square reference. The distance plot shows a dense central mass plus a visible set of large spikes, indicating a non-trivial group of multivariate shipment outliers rather than a few isolated points. This matches the estimated outlier share (`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * outlier_share_mcd)`%).

```{r}
# Compare log_lead_time for MCD outliers vs non-outliers
orders_mod %>%
  mutate(
    ship_outlier_mcd = factor(
      ship_outlier_mcd,
      levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
      labels = c("Non-outlier", "MCD outlier")
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ship_outlier_mcd, y = log_lead_time)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "log(lead time) for shipment MCD outliers vs others",
    x = "MCD outlier status",
    y = "log1p(days)"
  )
```
The boxplot compares log1p(lead_time) between orders flagged as multivariate shipment outliers by MCD and all other orders. MCD identifies a subset of orders with unusual shipment profiles, but their delivery times are not systematically extreme.

The medians and interquartile ranges of the two groups are very similar, and the overlap in whiskers and points is substantial. This indicates that although MCD outliers have unusual combinations of shipment characteristics, their delivery times are not systematically more extreme than the rest of the sample. Consequently, I keep these orders in the data and use robust-regression sensitivity plus mixed-model specification checks rather than deleting them.

## 5.2 Models Engineering

In this section, I treat the research questions as a sequence of modelling experiments using `orders_mod`:

- Variance decomposition (M0) to quantify how much variability in log‑lead time is attributable to sellers and customer states via random intercepts.

- Routing experiment (M1) to measure the effect of same‑state and same‑region shipments after accounting for the hierarchy.

- Shipment experiment (M2) to assess how standardized shipment characteristics (weight, volume, value, freight, items) explain remaining variation.

- Baseline full model (M3) adding seasonality, purchase year, and product themes.

Then I extend the baseline with cluster-informed heterogeneity models:
- `M4_c1`: add precluster main effects.
- `M4_c2`: add precluster interactions for key routing and shipment terms.

For interpretation, I use M3 as the reference baseline and `M4_c2` as the preferred heterogeneity specification.

### 5.2.1 M0: Null model

```{r}
# Mixed-effects models M0–M3
## Response: log_lead_time
## Random effects: seller_id, customer_state


##  Model M0 – Null model (variance decomposition)
# Why: quantify how much variation is at seller vs customer_state level.

mod_M0 <- lmer(
  log_lead_time ~ 1 +
    (1 | seller_id) +
    (1 | customer_state),
  data = orders_mod,
  REML = TRUE
)

summary(mod_M0)

# Variance components and ICC-style interpretation
VarCorr(mod_M0)
sigma_M0 <- sigma(mod_M0)^2  # residual variance
```



 This null model provides the baseline variance decomposition before any fixed predictors are added. It tells us how much delivery-time heterogeneity is attributable to seller-level and customer-state-level clustering versus within-group residual variation.

Random intercept variances:

Seller: 0.0589 (SD ≈ 0.243).

Customer state:0.0691 (SD ≈ 0.263).

Residual: 0.2316 (SD ≈ 0.481).


Interpretation:

- There is substantial variation in log‑lead time across both sellers and customer states even before adding any covariates.

- Roughly speaking, the between‑state variability is similar in magnitude to the between‑seller variability, which supports your variance‑decomposition RQ about hierarchy

Even without covariates, there is substantial heterogeneity in log‑lead time across both sellers and customer states, with between‑state and between‑seller variation of comparable magnitude.


### 5.2.2 M1: Add routing

```{r}
## Model M1 – Add routing (same state / same region)
# Why: test how much routing alone explains after accounting for hierarchy.

mod_M1 <- lmer(
  log_lead_time ~
    is_same_state + is_same_region +
    (1 | seller_id) +
    (1 | customer_state),
  data = orders_mod,
  REML = TRUE
)

summary(mod_M1)
```

Adding routing indicators (`is_same_state`, `is_same_region`) tests whether geography alone explains meaningful variation in lead time after accounting for random intercepts. A negative same-state effect is consistent with faster within-state delivery.

Key changes:

- Random‑effect variances shrink:

Seller SD: from 0.243 → 0.233.

State SD: from 0.263 → 0.207.

Residual SD: from 0.481 → 0.460.


- Routing coefficients:

is_same_stateTRUE ≈ -0.402, statistic significant.

is_same_regionTRUE ≈ -0.094 statistic significant



Interpretation:

- Negative sign means faster deliveries (lower log‑lead time) for same‑state and same‑region shipments.

- Effect sizes are large: same‑state alone corresponds roughly to exp(−0.40)≈0.67, i.e. about 33% shorter expected lead time, holding random effects fixed.

- Likelihood ratio test M0 vs M1: Chisquare ≈8358 on 2 df, p < 2.2e‑16 → routing explains a huge chunk of structured variation.

After including routing, same‑state shipments are on average about one‑third faster and same‑region shipments about 9% faster than cross‑region shipments, and routing alone explains roughly 14% of the variance in log‑lead time.


### 5.2.3 M2: Add shipment predictors
```{r}
##  Model M2 – Add shipment predictors
# Why: see how much of remaining variation is explained by shipment profile.

mod_M2 <- lmer(
  log_lead_time ~
    is_same_state + is_same_region +
    z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value + z_log_freight + z_log_items +
    (1 | seller_id) +
    (1 | customer_state),
  data = orders_mod,
  REML = TRUE
)

summary(mod_M2)
```

This model adds shipment characteristics (weight, volume, value, freight, items) on top of routing. Changes in coefficients and fit relative to M1 show how much shipment composition explains additional lead-time variation.

Key points:

Random‑effect SDs shrink further:

Seller: 0.233 → 0.228.

State: 0.207 → 0.186.

Residual: 0.460 → 0.459 (small change).


Shipment effects:

z_log_freight: strong positive (≈ 0.056, p < 2e‑16) → more expensive freight ↔ longer lead time, once routing is controlled.

z_log_items: strong negative (≈ -0.036, p < 2e‑16) → orders with more items (relative to typical) tend to be delivered faster, possibly reflecting batching or different logistics channels.

z_log_value: small positive but significant (≈ 0.009, p ≈ 0.002): higher‑value orders are slightly slower, conditional on other factors.

Shipment characteristics significantly refine the model: higher freight cost predicts slower deliveries, while orders with more items tend to be delivered slightly faster, possibly reflecting different consolidation and handling practices.


### 5.2.4 M3: Full model with time + product themes

```{r}
##Model M3 – Full model with time + themes
# Why: control for seasonality, calendar year, and product themes.

mod_M3 <- lmer(
  log_lead_time ~
    is_same_state + is_same_region +
    z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value + z_log_freight + z_log_items +
    season + purchase_year + theme_name +
    (1 | seller_id) +
    (1 | customer_state),
  data = orders_mod,
  REML = TRUE
)

summary(mod_M3)
```

```{r s523_m3_metrics}
vc_m2 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod_M2))
vc_m3 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod_M3))

sd_m2_seller <- vc_m2$sdcor[vc_m2$grp == "seller_id" & vc_m2$var1 == "(Intercept)"][1]
sd_m2_state <- vc_m2$sdcor[vc_m2$grp == "customer_state" & vc_m2$var1 == "(Intercept)"][1]
sd_m2_resid <- sigma(mod_M2)

sd_m3_seller <- vc_m3$sdcor[vc_m3$grp == "seller_id" & vc_m3$var1 == "(Intercept)"][1]
sd_m3_state <- vc_m3$sdcor[vc_m3$grp == "customer_state" & vc_m3$var1 == "(Intercept)"][1]
sd_m3_resid <- sigma(mod_M3)

m3_fixef_tbl <- broom.mixed::tidy(mod_M3, effects = "fixed")
m3_r2 <- performance::r2(mod_M3)
```

Comment (M3): this is the fully adjusted pooled baseline specification. It controls for time and product mix and provides the benchmark for cluster-conditioned heterogeneity in `M4_c1` and `M4_c2`.

- Random-effect dispersion continues to shrink from M2 to M3: seller SD `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_m2_seller)` \(\rightarrow\) `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_m3_seller)`, state SD `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_m2_state)` \(\rightarrow\) `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_m3_state)`, residual SD `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_m2_resid)` \(\rightarrow\) `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_m3_resid)`.
- Baseline fit is stronger in fixed effects: marginal \(R^2 = `r sprintf("%.3f", m3_r2$R2_marginal)`\), conditional \(R^2 = `r sprintf("%.3f", m3_r2$R2_conditional)`\).
- Core direction remains stable: same-state and same-region coefficients are negative; freight is positive; items are negative.
- Time controls remain informative, with faster delivery relative to DJF in MAM/JJA/SON and negative year dummies for 2017/2018 versus 2016.
- Theme effects are comparatively small versus routing and freight, so themes act mainly as adjustment controls rather than primary drivers.


### 5.2.5 M4: Full model with Cluster-informed heterogeneity

I now use the pre-model shipment clusters as a model-engineering diagnostic. The purpose is to test whether core effects in M3 (routing and shipment terms) are approximately constant across shipment regimes, or whether there is meaningful heterogeneity that should be acknowledged in interpretation.

```{r s54_cluster_setup}
orders_mod_cluster <- orders_mod %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(precluster)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(precluster = factor(precluster))

orders_mod_cluster %>%
  dplyr::count(precluster, name = "n_orders") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(pct_sample = 100 * n_orders / sum(n_orders))
```

```{r s54_cluster_models}
mod_M4_c1 <- lmer(
  log_lead_time ~
    is_same_state + is_same_region +
    z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value + z_log_freight + z_log_items +
    season + purchase_year + theme_name +
    precluster +
    (1 | seller_id) +
    (1 | customer_state),
  data = orders_mod_cluster,
  REML = TRUE
)

mod_M4_c2 <- lmer(
  log_lead_time ~
    is_same_state * precluster +
    is_same_region +
    z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value +
    z_log_freight * precluster +
    z_log_items * precluster +
    season + purchase_year + theme_name +
    (1 | seller_id) +
    (1 | customer_state),
  data = orders_mod_cluster,
  REML = TRUE
)
```

```{r s54_cluster_compare_table}
extract_r2_local <- function(model_obj) {
  r2_obj <- performance::r2(model_obj)
  tibble::tibble(
    r2_marginal = unname(r2_obj[["R2_marginal"]]),
    r2_conditional = unname(r2_obj[["R2_conditional"]])
  )
}

mod_M3_base_ML_cluster <- update(mod_M3, data = orders_mod_cluster, REML = FALSE)
mod_M4_c1_ML <- update(mod_M4_c1, REML = FALSE)
mod_M4_c2_ML <- update(mod_M4_c2, REML = FALSE)

cluster_model_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  model = c("M3_base", "M4_c1_precluster_main", "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"),
  AIC = c(AIC(mod_M3_base_ML_cluster), AIC(mod_M4_c1_ML), AIC(mod_M4_c2_ML)),
  BIC = c(BIC(mod_M3_base_ML_cluster), BIC(mod_M4_c1_ML), BIC(mod_M4_c2_ML)),
  logLik = c(as.numeric(logLik(mod_M3_base_ML_cluster)),
             as.numeric(logLik(mod_M4_c1_ML)),
             as.numeric(logLik(mod_M4_c2_ML)))
) %>%
  dplyr::bind_cols(dplyr::bind_rows(
    extract_r2_local(mod_M3),
    extract_r2_local(mod_M4_c1),
    extract_r2_local(mod_M4_c2)
  )) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    delta_AIC = AIC - min(AIC),
    delta_BIC = BIC - min(BIC)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(delta_AIC)

cluster_model_tbl
```

```{r s54_cluster_stratified_models}
cluster_key_terms <- c("is_same_stateTRUE", "is_same_regionTRUE", "z_log_freight", "z_log_items", "z_log_value")

fit_cluster_stratified <- function(cluster_label) {
  dat <- orders_mod_cluster %>%
    dplyr::filter(precluster == cluster_label)

  fit_try <- tryCatch(
    lmer(
      log_lead_time ~
        is_same_state + is_same_region +
        z_log_freight + z_log_items + z_log_value +
        season + purchase_year + theme_name +
        (1 | seller_id) + (1 | customer_state),
      data = dat,
      REML = TRUE
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  model_used <- "seller + state random intercepts"
  if (is.null(fit_try)) {
    fit_try <- tryCatch(
      lmer(
        log_lead_time ~
          is_same_state + is_same_region +
          z_log_freight + z_log_items + z_log_value +
          season + purchase_year + theme_name +
          (1 | seller_id),
        data = dat,
        REML = TRUE
      ),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    model_used <- "seller random intercept only"
  }

  if (is.null(fit_try)) {
    return(tibble::tibble(
      precluster = as.character(cluster_label),
      model_used = "fit_failed",
      term = NA_character_,
      estimate = NA_real_,
      std.error = NA_real_,
      conf.low = NA_real_,
      conf.high = NA_real_,
      p.value = NA_real_
    ))
  }

  broom.mixed::tidy(fit_try, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      precluster = as.character(cluster_label),
      model_used = model_used
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(precluster, model_used, term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)
}

cluster_stratified_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(levels(orders_mod_cluster$precluster), fit_cluster_stratified) %>%
  dplyr::filter(term %in% cluster_key_terms)

cluster_stratified_tbl
```

```{r s54_cluster_stratified_plot, fig.height=5.0, fig.width=9.2}
cluster_term_labels <- c(
  is_same_stateTRUE = "Same-state shipment",

  z_log_freight = "Freight cost (z log)",
  z_log_items = "Item count (z log)",
  z_log_value = "Order value (z log)"
)

plot_cluster_strata <- cluster_stratified_tbl %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    term_label = factor(cluster_term_labels[term], levels = rev(unname(cluster_term_labels))),
    precluster = factor(precluster, levels = sort(unique(precluster)))
  )

ggplot(plot_cluster_strata, aes(x = estimate, y = term_label, color = precluster)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.55), size = 2.1) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    width = 0,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.55),
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Cluster-stratified sensitivity of key fixed effects",
    subtitle = "Mixed-effects fits by pre-model shipment regime",
    x = "Coefficient estimate (log lead-time scale)",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Precluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Interpretation for this run:

- The selected partition (`K = `r k_final_pre`) is usable for mixed modelling: cluster shares range from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(precluster_summary$pct_sample, na.rm = TRUE))`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(precluster_summary$pct_sample, na.rm = TRUE))`%.
- Adding cluster main effects (`M4_c1`) improves fit versus M3 (\(\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_base_vs_M4_c1$Chisq[2])`\), \(df = `r lrt_base_vs_M4_c1$Df[2]`\), p `r {pv <- format.pval(lrt_base_vs_M4_c1[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16); if (startsWith(pv, "<")) pv else paste0("= ", pv)}`).
- Adding interactions (`M4_c2`) gives a much larger gain (\(\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.1f", lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2$Chisq[2])`\), \(df = `r lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2$Df[2]`\), p `r {pv <- format.pval(lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16); if (startsWith(pv, "<")) pv else paste0("= ", pv)}`) and improves AIC/BIC from `r sprintf("%.0f", cluster_model_tbl$AIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"])`/`r sprintf("%.0f", cluster_model_tbl$BIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"])` to `r sprintf("%.0f", cluster_model_tbl$AIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"])`/`r sprintf("%.0f", cluster_model_tbl$BIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"])`.
- Marginal \(R^2\) increases from `r sprintf("%.3f", cluster_model_tbl$r2_marginal[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"])` (M3) to `r sprintf("%.3f", cluster_model_tbl$r2_marginal[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"])` (M4\_c2), while conditional \(R^2\) moves from `r sprintf("%.3f", cluster_model_tbl$r2_conditional[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", cluster_model_tbl$r2_conditional[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"])`.
- Direction is stable but magnitude is regime-specific: same-state effects are negative in every cluster (`r sprintf("%.3f", min(cluster_stratified_tbl$estimate[cluster_stratified_tbl$term == "is_same_stateTRUE"], na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(cluster_stratified_tbl$estimate[cluster_stratified_tbl$term == "is_same_stateTRUE"], na.rm = TRUE))`), while freight effects stay positive (`r sprintf("%.3f", min(cluster_stratified_tbl$estimate[cluster_stratified_tbl$term == "z_log_freight"], na.rm = TRUE))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(cluster_stratified_tbl$estimate[cluster_stratified_tbl$term == "z_log_freight"], na.rm = TRUE))`).
  
## 5.3 Model comparison and final selection

```{r}
# Likelihood ratio test M0 vs M1 (REML off for fair comparison)
mod_M0_ML <- update(mod_M0, REML = FALSE)
mod_M1_ML <- update(mod_M1, REML = FALSE)
lrt_M0_M1 <- anova(mod_M0_ML, mod_M1_ML)
lrt_M0_M1

mod_M2_ML <- update(mod_M2, REML = FALSE)
lrt_M1_M2 <- anova(mod_M1_ML, mod_M2_ML)
lrt_M1_M2

mod_M3_ML <- update(mod_M3, REML = FALSE)
lrt_M2_M3 <- anova(mod_M2_ML, mod_M3_ML)
lrt_M2_M3

# M3 vs M4 comparison on common cluster-ready sample
lrt_base_vs_M4_c1
lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2
```

Model comparison takeaway:

- M1 \(\rightarrow\) M2 is strongly supported (\(\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.1f", lrt_M1_M2$Chisq[2])`\), \(df = `r lrt_M1_M2$Df[2]`\), p `r {pv <- format.pval(lrt_M1_M2[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16); if (startsWith(pv, "<")) pv else paste0("= ", pv)}`); shipment variables add clear explanatory value beyond routing.
- M2 \(\rightarrow\) M3 is also strongly supported (\(\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.1f", lrt_M2_M3$Chisq[2])`\), \(df = `r lrt_M2_M3$Df[2]`\), p `r {pv <- format.pval(lrt_M2_M3[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16); if (startsWith(pv, "<")) pv else paste0("= ", pv)}`); time and theme controls matter materially.
- On the common cluster-ready sample, M3 \(\rightarrow\) M4\_c1 and M4\_c1 \(\rightarrow\) M4\_c2 are both decisively supported (`r format.pval(lrt_base_vs_M4_c1[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16)` and `r format.pval(lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16)`), confirming non-trivial cluster-conditioned heterogeneity.
- Final choice: `M4_c2_cluster_interactions` is the preferred inferential model; M3 remains the pooled baseline comparator.

R² evolution (marginal vs conditional):

- M0: `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_marginal[model_compare_tbl$model == "M0"])` / `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_conditional[model_compare_tbl$model == "M0"])`.
- M1: `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_marginal[model_compare_tbl$model == "M1"])` / `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_conditional[model_compare_tbl$model == "M1"])`.
- M2: `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_marginal[model_compare_tbl$model == "M2"])` / `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_conditional[model_compare_tbl$model == "M2"])`.
- M3: `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_marginal[model_compare_tbl$model == "M3"])` / `r sprintf("%.3f", model_compare_tbl$r2_conditional[model_compare_tbl$model == "M3"])`.

In plain terms, hierarchy explains a large base share, routing gives the first major fixed-effects jump, shipment terms add incremental refinement, and time/theme controls add the final substantial gain in the pooled baseline.


```{r}
# Simple residual diagnostics for M3
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fitted(mod_M3), resid(mod_M3),
     pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "M3: Residuals vs Fitted")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

qqnorm(resid(mod_M3), main = "M3: Residual QQ-plot")
qqline(resid(mod_M3), col = "red", lty = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

From the residual vs fitted and residual QQ‑plot for M3:

Residual vs fitted: cloud is roughly symmetric around zero, with no strong funnel shape or obvious non‑linear pattern → variance is reasonably stable across the fitted range.


Residual QQ‑plot: middle of the distribution lies close to the 45° line, but the upper tail bends upwards (a few residuals much larger than Gaussian) and lower tail slightly downwards.

→ The log transformation handled most skewness, but there remain heavy tails and a small number of large residuals.

These diagnostics suggest that the log‑mixed model captures most systematic structure, but residuals remain heavy‑tailed, reinforcing the need for the robust and trimming experiments planned in the next section.

Conclusion:
Across models M0–M3, hierarchy, routing, shipment features, and time controls explain a substantial share of variability in log‑delivery lead time. The M4 extensions then show that key routing and freight effects are heterogeneous across shipment regimes, with large fit gains relative to the pooled M3 baseline. Residuals remain heavy‑tailed, and multivariate shipment outliers are non-trivial, so the next section stress-tests inference with robust flat estimators, mixed-model variants, regional refits, and bootstrap intervals.

Model-engineering conclusion:

- Cluster-informed heterogeneity is not only descriptive; it materially improves model fit and changes substantive interpretation of effect sizes.
- `M4_c2_cluster_interactions` is the preferred inferential model in this run because it strongly outperforms both `M3_base` and `M4_c1_precluster_main` on likelihood and information criteria, while improving marginal \(R^2\).
- Section 6 therefore stress-tests `M4_c2` directly.

# 6. Robustness & Bootstrap Analysis

**Observation:** Section 5 models fit well overall, but tails and influential profiles remain visible.

**Risk:** A small subset of atypical orders or sellers could distort fixed-effect inference and subgroup interpretation.

**Experiment design:** I run a sequence of sensitivity experiments on the same modelling sample: robust flat regressions, trimmed/variant mixed models, region-wise mixed models, and bootstrap uncertainty checks.

**Decision rule:** I treat conclusions as robust when key effect signs remain stable and effect magnitudes/CIs change only modestly across these stress tests.

This robustness section is anchored on the preferred M4\_c2 specification.

```{r s6_setup_objects}
s6_data <- orders_mod_cluster
s6_model_ref <- mod_M4_c2

s6_core_terms <- c(
  "is_same_stateTRUE",
  "is_same_regionTRUE",
  "z_log_freight",
  "z_log_items",
  "z_log_value"
)

s6_terms_compare <- c(
  "is_same_stateTRUE",
  "is_same_regionTRUE",
  "z_log_freight",
  "z_log_items",
  "is_same_stateTRUE:precluster5",
  "precluster5:z_log_freight",
  "seasonJJA"
)

s6_fixed_terms <- paste(
  "is_same_state * precluster + is_same_region +",
  "z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value + z_log_freight * precluster + z_log_items * precluster +",
  "season + purchase_year + theme_name"
)

s6_fixed_terms_no_theme <- paste(
  "is_same_state * precluster + is_same_region +",
  "z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value + z_log_freight * precluster + z_log_items * precluster +",
  "season + purchase_year"
)

tibble::tibble(
  n_orders = nrow(s6_data),
  n_sellers = dplyr::n_distinct(s6_data$seller_id),
  n_customer_states = dplyr::n_distinct(s6_data$customer_state),
  n_preclusters = dplyr::n_distinct(s6_data$precluster)
)
```

**Observation:** Delivery lead times are right-skewed with a long upper tail, residuals remain mildly heavy-tailed after log transformation, and some shipment/seller profiles are clearly atypical.

**Risk:** Classical estimates can be over-influenced by these tails/outliers.

```{r s6_tail_profile}
lead_quantiles <- stats::quantile(
  s6_data$lead_time_days_raw,
  probs = c(0.50, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

std_resid <- as.numeric(scale(residuals(s6_model_ref)))
tail_share_25 <- mean(abs(std_resid) > 2.5, na.rm = TRUE)
tail_share_30 <- mean(abs(std_resid) > 3.0, na.rm = TRUE)

outlier_share_mcd <- if ("ship_outlier_mcd" %in% names(s6_data)) {
  mean(s6_data$ship_outlier_mcd, na.rm = TRUE)
} else {
  NA_real_
}

seller_re <- ranef(s6_model_ref)$seller_id[[1]]
seller_re_quantiles <- stats::quantile(seller_re, probs = c(0.01, 0.50, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)

list(
  lead_time_quantiles_days = lead_quantiles,
  residual_tail_share_abs_gt_2_5 = tail_share_25,
  residual_tail_share_abs_gt_3_0 = tail_share_30,
  shipment_mcd_outlier_share = outlier_share_mcd,
  seller_random_intercept_quantiles = seller_re_quantiles
)
```

**Experiment framing (AMS-consistent):** These diagnostics match the robust-settings from class (heavy tails, vertical outliers, leverage risk), so each subsection below tests whether the main effects survive alternative estimators and perturbations.

## 6.1 Robust regression on flat models
**Observation:** Flat-model residuals show mild heavy tails and possible influential points.

**Risk:** OLS coefficients may be sensitive to vertical outliers/bad leverage.

**Experiment:** Refit the same flat specification with Huber M-estimation and LTS, then compare key coefficients against OLS.

**Decision rule:** If signs are unchanged and absolute differences are small, I treat flat-model conclusions as robust.

```{r s6_robust_flat_models, cache=TRUE}
flat_formula <- log_lead_time ~
  is_same_state + is_same_region +
  z_log_wgt + z_log_vol + z_log_value + z_log_freight + z_log_items

flat_data <- s6_data %>%
  dplyr::select(
    log_lead_time, is_same_state, is_same_region,
    z_log_wgt, z_log_vol, z_log_value, z_log_freight, z_log_items
  ) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na()

fit_flat_ols <- lm(flat_formula, data = flat_data)
fit_flat_huber <- robustbase::lmrob(flat_formula, data = flat_data, setting = "KS2014")
fit_flat_lts <- robustbase::ltsReg(flat_formula, data = flat_data, alpha = 0.75, nsamp = 500)

coef_compare_flat <- tibble::tibble(
  term = s6_core_terms,
  ols = unname(coef(fit_flat_ols)[s6_core_terms]),
  huber_m = unname(coef(fit_flat_huber)[s6_core_terms]),
  lts = unname(coef(fit_flat_lts)[s6_core_terms])
) %>%
  mutate(
    abs_diff_huber_vs_ols = abs(huber_m - ols),
    abs_diff_lts_vs_ols = abs(lts - ols)
  )

coef_compare_flat
```

```{r s6_plot_flat_coef_stability, fig.height=4.8, fig.width=8}
term_labels <- c(
  is_same_stateTRUE = "Same-state shipment",
  is_same_regionTRUE = "Same-region shipment",
  z_log_freight = "Freight cost (z log)",
  z_log_items = "Item count (z log)",
  z_log_value = "Order value (z log)"
)

coef_flat_plot <- coef_compare_flat %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ols, huber_m, lts),
    names_to = "model",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c("ols", "huber_m", "lts"),
      labels = c("OLS", "Huber M", "LTS")
    ),
    term_label = term_labels[term],
    term_label = factor(term_label, levels = rev(unname(term_labels)))
  )

coef_flat_span <- coef_flat_plot %>%
  dplyr::group_by(term_label) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    min_est = min(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_est = max(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(coef_flat_plot, aes(x = estimate, y = term_label, color = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_segment(
    data = coef_flat_span,
    aes(x = min_est, xend = max_est, y = term_label, yend = term_label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), size = 2.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Section 6.1: Coefficient stability across OLS and robust estimators",
    x = "Estimate on log-lead-time scale",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

- Magnitudes: for all five core terms, robust estimates differ from OLS by only a few hundredths of a log-unit.
- Direction: signs are identical across OLS, Huber M, and LTS for same-state, same-region, freight, items, and value, so outliers do not flip substantive conclusions.
- Routing strength: same-state coefficients remain large and negative across estimators, confirming a stable same-state speed advantage.
- Plot reading: OLS, Huber M, and LTS points for each term lie close together and on the same side of zero.
- Max drift benchmark: the largest absolute robust-vs-OLS difference is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(c(coef_compare_flat$abs_diff_huber_vs_ols, coef_compare_flat$abs_diff_lts_vs_ols), na.rm = TRUE))`.

**Result/decision:** The robust and OLS estimates stay closely aligned, so the 6.1 robustness criterion is supported.

## 6.2 Trimming and variant mixed‑effects fits

**Observation:** The outcome has a long upper tail, and mixed-model conclusions could depend on tail handling or modelling choices.

**Risk:** Main effects may be model-dependent (specific random-effects structure or control set).

**Experiment:** Stress-test M4\_c2 with (i) 95th-percentile trimming, (ii) removing theme controls, and (iii) seller-only random effects; compare fixed effects and variance components.

**Decision rule:** If key terms remain same-sign with modest coefficient drift, multilevel conclusions are considered stable.

```{r s6_trimmed_and_variant_lmm, cache=TRUE}
cut95 <- stats::quantile(s6_data$lead_time_days_raw, probs = 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

orders_mod_trim <- s6_data %>%
  mutate(
    lead_time_days_trim95 = pmin(lead_time_days_raw, cut95),
    log_lead_trim95 = log1p(lead_time_days_trim95)
  )

formula_m4_trim95 <- as.formula(
  paste0(
    "log_lead_trim95 ~ ", s6_fixed_terms,
    " + (1 | seller_id) + (1 | customer_state)"
  )
)

formula_m4_no_theme <- as.formula(
  paste0(
    "log_lead_time ~ ", s6_fixed_terms_no_theme,
    " + (1 | seller_id) + (1 | customer_state)"
  )
)

formula_m4_seller_only <- as.formula(
  paste0(
    "log_lead_time ~ ", s6_fixed_terms,
    " + (1 | seller_id)"
  )
)

mod_M4_c2_ML <- update(mod_M4_c2, REML = FALSE)
mod_M4_trim95 <- lmer(formula_m4_trim95, data = orders_mod_trim, REML = FALSE)
mod_M4_no_theme <- lmer(formula_m4_no_theme, data = s6_data, REML = FALSE)
mod_M4_seller_only <- lmer(formula_m4_seller_only, data = s6_data, REML = FALSE)

safe_extract_fixef <- function(model, terms) {
  cf <- fixef(model)
  out <- rep(NA_real_, length(terms))
  names(out) <- terms
  out[intersect(terms, names(cf))] <- cf[intersect(terms, names(cf))]
  unname(out)
}

coef_compare_m4_variants <- tibble::tibble(
  term = s6_terms_compare,
  m4_main = safe_extract_fixef(mod_M4_c2_ML, s6_terms_compare),
  m4_trim95 = safe_extract_fixef(mod_M4_trim95, s6_terms_compare),
  m4_no_theme = safe_extract_fixef(mod_M4_no_theme, s6_terms_compare),
  m4_seller_only = safe_extract_fixef(mod_M4_seller_only, s6_terms_compare)
) %>%
  mutate(
    abs_diff_trim95 = abs(m4_trim95 - m4_main),
    abs_diff_no_theme = abs(m4_no_theme - m4_main),
    abs_diff_seller_only = abs(m4_seller_only - m4_main)
  )

get_re_var <- function(model, grp_name) {
  vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
  hit <- vc$grp == grp_name & vc$var1 == "(Intercept)"
  if (any(hit)) vc$vcov[which(hit)[1]] else NA_real_
}

var_compare <- tibble::tibble(
  model = c("M4_c2_main", "M4_trim95", "M4_no_theme", "M4_seller_only"),
  seller_intercept_var = c(
    get_re_var(mod_M4_c2_ML, "seller_id"),
    get_re_var(mod_M4_trim95, "seller_id"),
    get_re_var(mod_M4_no_theme, "seller_id"),
    get_re_var(mod_M4_seller_only, "seller_id")
  ),
  customer_state_intercept_var = c(
    get_re_var(mod_M4_c2_ML, "customer_state"),
    get_re_var(mod_M4_trim95, "customer_state"),
    get_re_var(mod_M4_no_theme, "customer_state"),
    get_re_var(mod_M4_seller_only, "customer_state")
  ),
  residual_var = c(
    sigma(mod_M4_c2_ML)^2,
    sigma(mod_M4_trim95)^2,
    sigma(mod_M4_no_theme)^2,
    sigma(mod_M4_seller_only)^2
  )
)

list(
  coefficient_stability = coef_compare_m4_variants,
  random_effect_variance_stability = var_compare
)
```

```{r s6_plot_lmm_sensitivity, fig.height=5.2, fig.width=9}
delta_plot <- coef_compare_m4_variants %>%
  dplyr::select(term, abs_diff_trim95, abs_diff_no_theme, abs_diff_seller_only) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("abs_diff_"),
    names_to = "variant",
    values_to = "abs_delta"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    variant = factor(
      variant,
      levels = c("abs_diff_trim95", "abs_diff_no_theme", "abs_diff_seller_only"),
      labels = c("Trim at 95th percentile", "Remove theme controls", "Seller random effect only")
    ),
    term_label = dplyr::recode(
      term,
      is_same_stateTRUE = "Same-state shipment",
      is_same_regionTRUE = "Same-region shipment",
      z_log_freight = "Freight cost",
      z_log_items = "Item count",
      `is_same_stateTRUE:precluster5` = "Same-state × cluster 5",
      `precluster5:z_log_freight` = "Freight × cluster 5",
      seasonJJA = "Season: JJA"
    ),
    term_label = factor(term_label, levels = rev(c(
      "Same-state shipment",
      "Same-region shipment",
      "Freight cost",
      "Item count",
      "Same-state × cluster 5",
      "Freight × cluster 5",
      "Season: JJA"
    )))
  )

ggplot(delta_plot, aes(x = variant, y = term_label, fill = abs_delta)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f1f5f9", high = "#0f766e") +
  labs(
    title = "Section 6.2: Sensitivity heatmap (absolute coefficient change vs M4_c2)",
    x = NULL,

    fill = "|Delta|"

```

- Trim and specification stress tests: moving from main M4\_c2 to trimmed and structure-variant models shifts key coefficients only modestly, and core signs stay unchanged.
- Same-state effect: the coefficient remains clearly negative across all tested variants, so the routing conclusion is stable.
- Freight and items: freight remains positive and items remains negative, with relatively small drift versus the main model.
- Variance components: residual variance declines under trimming and random-effect variances shrink slightly in variants, but seller and customer-state heterogeneity remain non-zero.
- Plot reading (heatmap): mostly light tiles indicate small absolute coefficient deltas versus M4\_c2, with larger movement concentrated in a minority of term-variant cells.
- Max drift benchmark: the largest absolute coefficient delta across mixed-model variants is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(c(coef_compare_m4_variants$abs_diff_trim95, coef_compare_m4_variants$abs_diff_no_theme, coef_compare_m4_variants$abs_diff_seller_only), na.rm = TRUE))`.

**Result/decision:** Coefficient drift across variants is limited and core signs persist, so the 6.2 stability criterion is supported.

## 6.3 Region‑specific models

**Observation:** Brazil is geographically heterogeneous, so pooled effects may hide regional differences.

**Risk:** Main conclusions could be driven by one or two dominant regions rather than being transportable.

**Experiment:** Refit simplified mixed models by customer macro-region and compare effect direction/magnitude against national estimates.

**Decision rule:** If key effects keep the same sign across regions with moderate magnitude shifts, transportability is supported.

```{r s6_region_specific_lmm, cache=TRUE}
regions <- c("North", "Northeast", "Central-West", "Southeast", "South")
region_terms <- c("is_same_stateTRUE", "z_log_freight", "z_log_items", "z_log_value")

region_fit <- lapply(regions, function(reg) {
  dat_reg <- s6_data %>% filter(customer_region == reg)

  meta <- tibble::tibble(
    customer_region = reg,
    n_orders = nrow(dat_reg),
    n_sellers = dplyr::n_distinct(dat_reg$seller_id),
    n_same_state = sum(dat_reg$is_same_state %in% TRUE, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_diff_state = sum(dat_reg$is_same_state %in% FALSE, na.rm = TRUE),
    estimable_same_state = dplyr::n_distinct(dat_reg$is_same_state) >= 2L
  )

  if (nrow(dat_reg) < 100L || dplyr::n_distinct(dat_reg$is_same_state) < 2L) {
    return(list(meta = meta %>% mutate(note = "Skipped: insufficient variation"), coef = tibble::tibble()))
  }

  fit_reg <- tryCatch(
    lmer(
      log_lead_time ~ is_same_state + z_log_value + z_log_freight + z_log_items + (1 | seller_id),
      data = dat_reg,
      REML = FALSE
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  if (is.null(fit_reg)) {
    return(list(meta = meta %>% mutate(note = "Fit failed"), coef = tibble::tibble()))
  }

  coef_tbl <- broom.mixed::tidy(
    fit_reg,
    effects = "fixed",
    conf.int = TRUE,
    conf.method = "Wald"
  ) %>%
    filter(term %in% region_terms) %>%
    mutate(customer_region = reg)

  list(meta = meta %>% mutate(note = NA_character_), coef = coef_tbl)
})

region_meta <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(region_fit, `[[`, "meta"))
region_coef <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(region_fit, `[[`, "coef")) %>%
  dplyr::select(customer_region, term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high)

region_sign_check <- region_coef %>%
  dplyr::group_by(term) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    min_estimate = min(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_estimate = max(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    same_sign_across_regions = (min_estimate > 0 & max_estimate > 0) | (min_estimate < 0 & max_estimate < 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

list(
  region_sample_sizes = region_meta,
  region_coefficients = region_coef,
  sign_stability = region_sign_check
)
```

```{r s6_plot_region_forest, fig.height=5.8, fig.width=9}
region_labels <- c(
  is_same_stateTRUE = "Same-state shipment",
  z_log_freight = "Freight cost",
  z_log_items = "Item count",
  z_log_value = "Order value"
)

region_plot_df <- region_coef %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    customer_region = factor(customer_region, levels = regions),
    term_label = region_labels[term]
  )

national_ref <- tibble::tibble(
  term = names(region_labels),
  term_label = unname(region_labels),
  national_estimate = unname(fixef(s6_model_ref)[names(region_labels)])
)

ggplot(region_plot_df, aes(x = customer_region, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(
    data = national_ref,
    aes(yintercept = national_estimate),
    color = "grey35",
    linetype = 3
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), color = "#0f766e") +
  facet_wrap(~ term_label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Section 6.3: Region-specific effects with national reference lines",
    x = "Customer macro-region",
    y = "Estimate on log-lead-time scale"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

- Across macro-regions, same-state estimates remain negative and freight estimates positive, so the direction of routing and shipment-cost effects is stable nationwide.
- Regions with longer average shipping distances (for example North and Northeast) tend to show larger same-state effects, which is coherent with geography rather than contradictory.

**Result/decision:** Regional fits preserve the main effect directions, so the 6.3 transportability criterion is supported.

## 6.4 Bootstrap uncertainty for the final mixed model
**Observation:** Mixed-model inference relies on asymptotic approximations that may be imperfect under mild non-normality.

**Risk:** Standard Wald intervals could understate uncertainty.

**Experiment:** Run parametric bootstrap for the final mixed model, report percentile CIs for key fixed effects as the primary inference, and compare with normal-approximation (Wald) CIs.

**Decision rule:** If percentile and Wald intervals largely overlap and imply the same substantive interpretation, inference is considered stable.

```{r s6_bootstrap_fixed_effects, cache=TRUE}
boot_terms <- c(
  "is_same_stateTRUE",
  "is_same_regionTRUE",
  "z_log_freight",
  "is_same_stateTRUE:precluster5",
  "precluster5:z_log_freight"
)
boot_fun <- function(fit) unname(fixef(fit)[boot_terms])

set.seed(42)
boot_nsim <- 80L
boot_m4 <- lme4::bootMer(
  mod_M4_c2,
  FUN = boot_fun,
  nsim = boot_nsim,
  type = "parametric",
  use.u = FALSE,
  parallel = "no"
)

boot_rep <- as.data.frame(boot_m4$t)
colnames(boot_rep) <- boot_terms

boot_ci_tbl <- purrr::map_dfr(boot_terms, function(term_name) {
  vals <- boot_rep[[term_name]]
  tibble::tibble(
    term = term_name,
    point_estimate = fixef(mod_M4_c2)[term_name],
    boot_mean = mean(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    boot_sd = sd(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    boot_perc_low = as.numeric(stats::quantile(vals, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)),
    boot_perc_high = as.numeric(stats::quantile(vals, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
})

wald_ci <- as.data.frame(confint(mod_M4_c2, parm = boot_terms, method = "Wald")) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  rename(wald_low = `2.5 %`, wald_high = `97.5 %`)

boot_vs_wald <- boot_ci_tbl %>%
  left_join(wald_ci, by = "term") %>%
  mutate(
    interval_overlap = pmax(boot_perc_low, wald_low) <= pmin(boot_perc_high, wald_high),
    low_diff_boot_minus_wald = boot_perc_low - wald_low,
    high_diff_boot_minus_wald = boot_perc_high - wald_high
  )

boot_vs_wald
```

```{r s6_plot_bootstrap_wald, fig.height=4.8, fig.width=8.8}
ci_labels <- c(
  is_same_stateTRUE = "Same-state shipment",
  is_same_regionTRUE = "Same-region shipment",
  z_log_freight = "Freight cost",
  `is_same_stateTRUE:precluster5` = "Same-state × cluster 5",
  `precluster5:z_log_freight` = "Freight × cluster 5"
)

ci_plot_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  boot_vs_wald %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      term,
      method = "Bootstrap percentile",
      estimate = point_estimate,
      low = boot_perc_low,
      high = boot_perc_high
    ),
  boot_vs_wald %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      term,
      method = "Wald",
      estimate = point_estimate,
      low = wald_low,
      high = wald_high
    )
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    term_label = ci_labels[term],
    term_label = factor(term_label, levels = rev(unname(ci_labels))),
    method = factor(method, levels = c("Bootstrap percentile", "Wald"))
  )

ggplot(ci_plot_df, aes(y = term_label, x = estimate, color = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(xmin = low, xmax = high),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.55),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Section 6.4: Bootstrap vs Wald confidence intervals",
    x = "Estimate and 95% interval",
    y = NULL,
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

- Interval width: bootstrap percentile and Wald 95% intervals are nearly identical for all key terms, with only very small endpoint differences.
- Overlap: intervals fully overlap for each key term and lead to the same significance conclusions.
- Centering: bootstrap intervals are centered close to the model point estimates, suggesting no material bootstrap-detected bias.
- Plot reading: bootstrap and Wald bars nearly overlap term-by-term in the CI plot, confirming a consistent uncertainty story.
- Overlap score: `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(boot_vs_wald$interval_overlap, na.rm = TRUE))`% of term-level intervals overlap.

**Result/decision:** Bootstrap and Wald intervals are highly consistent, so the 6.4 uncertainty criterion is supported.

## 6.5 Robustness verdict summary

```{r s6_robustness_verdict_table}
safe_max <- function(x) {
  if (all(is.na(x))) return(NA_real_)
  max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

flat_max_delta <- safe_max(c(
  coef_compare_flat$abs_diff_huber_vs_ols,
  coef_compare_flat$abs_diff_lts_vs_ols
))

lmm_max_delta <- safe_max(c(
  coef_compare_m4_variants$abs_diff_trim95,
  coef_compare_m4_variants$abs_diff_no_theme,
  coef_compare_m4_variants$abs_diff_seller_only
))

region_sign_share <- mean(region_sign_check$same_sign_across_regions, na.rm = TRUE)
ci_overlap_share <- mean(boot_vs_wald$interval_overlap, na.rm = TRUE)

robustness_verdict <- tibble::tibble(
  check = c(
    "Flat robust estimators",
    "Mixed-model variants",
    "Region-specific consistency",
    "Bootstrap vs Wald intervals"
  ),
  metric = c(
    "Max |Delta| vs OLS",
    "Max |Delta| vs baseline M4_c2",
    "Share of terms with same sign across regions",
    "Share of terms with CI overlap"
  ),
  value = c(flat_max_delta, lmm_max_delta, region_sign_share, ci_overlap_share),
  threshold = c("< 0.02", "< 0.03", ">= 0.75", ">= 0.80")
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    verdict = dplyr::case_when(
      check == "Flat robust estimators" & value < 0.02 ~ "PASS",
      check == "Mixed-model variants" & value < 0.03 ~ "PASS",
      check == "Region-specific consistency" & value >= 0.75 ~ "PASS",
      check == "Bootstrap vs Wald intervals" & value >= 0.80 ~ "PASS",
      TRUE ~ "REVIEW"
    ),
    value = round(value, 3)
  )

robustness_verdict
```

```{r s7_summary_metrics}
get_intercept_var <- function(model, grp_name) {
  vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
  hit <- vc$grp == grp_name & vc$var1 == "(Intercept)"
  if (any(hit)) vc$vcov[which(hit)[1]] else NA_real_
}

n_orders_final <- nrow(orders_mod_cluster)

m3_seller_var <- get_intercept_var(mod_M3, "seller_id")
m3_state_var <- get_intercept_var(mod_M3, "customer_state")
m3_resid_var <- sigma(mod_M3)^2
m3_total_var <- m3_seller_var + m3_state_var + m3_resid_var
m3_higher_level_share <- 100 * (m3_seller_var + m3_state_var) / m3_total_var

m3_aic <- cluster_model_tbl$AIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"]
m3_bic <- cluster_model_tbl$BIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"]
m4_aic <- cluster_model_tbl$AIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"]
m4_bic <- cluster_model_tbl$BIC[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"]
m3_r2_marg <- cluster_model_tbl$r2_marginal[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M3_base"]
m4_r2_marg <- cluster_model_tbl$r2_marginal[cluster_model_tbl$model == "M4_c2_cluster_interactions"]

same_state_range <- range(
  cluster_stratified_tbl$estimate[cluster_stratified_tbl$term == "is_same_stateTRUE"],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
freight_range <- range(
  cluster_stratified_tbl$estimate[cluster_stratified_tbl$term == "z_log_freight"],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

# 7. Key Findings and Discussion

## 7.1 Research questions and main patterns
This study addressed three linked questions: variance decomposition under hierarchy (RQ1), fixed-effect drivers of delivery time (RQ2), and robustness under outliers and re-specification (RQ3). On `r scales::comma(n_orders_final)` orders, the M0→M3 ladder established the pooled multilevel baseline, and M4 showed that part of the fixed-effect story is cluster-conditioned rather than constant. The core message is consistent: routing dominates, shipment features refine, and seller/state clustering remains material.

## 7.2 Seller and destination heterogeneity
Even after adjustment for route, shipment profile, season, and theme, meaningful between-group heterogeneity remains. In M3, seller random-intercept variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", m3_seller_var)`, customer-state variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", m3_state_var)`, and residual variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", m3_resid_var)` on the log scale. This means about `r sprintf("%.1f", m3_higher_level_share)`% of total variance still sits at higher levels, which keeps the multilevel specification empirically justified.

## 7.3 Routing and shipment effects with magnitudes
Routing remains the dominant operational lever, but M4 confirms that effects are not homogeneous across shipment regimes. Relative to M3, adding precluster main effects (M4\_c1) improves fit (\(\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.2f", lrt_base_vs_M4_c1$Chisq[2])`\), \(df = `r lrt_base_vs_M4_c1$Df[2]`\), p `r {pv <- format.pval(lrt_base_vs_M4_c1[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16); if (startsWith(pv, "<")) pv else paste0("= ", pv)}`). Adding interactions (M4\_c2) gives a much larger gain (\(\chi^2 = `r sprintf("%.1f", lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2$Chisq[2])`\), \(df = `r lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2$Df[2]`\), p `r {pv <- format.pval(lrt_M4_c1_vs_M4_c2[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16); if (startsWith(pv, "<")) pv else paste0("= ", pv)}`), with AIC/BIC moving from `r sprintf("%.0f", m3_aic)`/`r sprintf("%.0f", m3_bic)` to `r sprintf("%.0f", m4_aic)`/`r sprintf("%.0f", m4_bic)`. Marginal \(R^2\) rises from `r sprintf("%.3f", m3_r2_marg)` to `r sprintf("%.3f", m4_r2_marg)`.

The direction of key effects stays stable, but magnitudes vary by regime: same-state coefficients range from `r sprintf("%.3f", same_state_range[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", same_state_range[2])`, while freight coefficients range from `r sprintf("%.3f", freight_range[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", freight_range[2])`. A pooled coefficient is still useful as an average, but it masks meaningful operational heterogeneity.

## 7.4 Robustness and credibility of the results
A full robustness battery suggests the conclusions are not driven by a few extreme orders or by one modelling choice. MCD diagnostics flag about `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * outlier_share_mcd)`% of shipment-profile outliers, but robust flat fits preserve OLS directions with max drift `r sprintf("%.3f", flat_max_delta)`. Mixed-model stress tests (trim95, no-theme, seller-only) keep core signs with max drift `r sprintf("%.3f", lmm_max_delta)`. Region-specific models preserve effect direction for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * region_sign_share)`% of tracked terms, and bootstrap-vs-Wald intervals overlap for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * ci_overlap_share)`% of terms.

Overall, the robustness evidence is strong for effect direction and acceptable for effect magnitude. The practical interpretation is cautious but clear: ordering of effects is stable, while exact coefficient size remains moderately specification-sensitive.

## 7.5 Managerial implications and limitations
From an applied perspective, the results point to three priorities. First, local/regional routing remains the largest controllable lever, so inventory positioning and seller-matching rules should maximize same-state fulfillment when feasible. Second, ETA models should be regime-aware: M4 results indicate that freight and routing effects vary materially across shipment profiles, so one global SLA rule is suboptimal. Third, seller/state random-effect dispersion remains substantial after adjustment, so platform operations should keep explicit seller-performance monitoring and targeted support for slow-tail sellers.

Limitations remain clear. The study is observational and single-platform, so coefficients are associational. Key operational variables (carrier contracts, warehouse network, route congestion, fulfillment cut-off discipline) are unobserved and likely absorb into seller/state effects. Preclusters are also model-based constructs from observed shipment features, useful for heterogeneity engineering but not latent causal classes. Future work should test random-slope multilevel variants, richer robust likelihoods, and external validation on a different period or marketplace.
